topic.title: React & Next.js
topic.summary: How React turns state into UI, the hooks every interview probes (useEffect, useMemo, useCallback, custom hooks), and the Next.js App Router ideas: rendering strategies and Server vs Client Components.
topic.overview:
## What interviewers expect
If React or Next.js is on your CV, expect three kinds of questions:

1. **How React works** — the Virtual DOM and reconciliation, why keys matter, what triggers a re-render, props vs state.
2. **Hooks in practice** — `useEffect` dependencies and cleanup, Strict Mode's double effect, `useMemo`/`useCallback`/`memo`, writing a custom hook (often `useFetch` or `useDebounce`) live.
3. **Architecture and Next.js** — where state should live (Context vs Zustand/Redux vs TanStack Query), CSR vs SSR vs SSG vs ISR, Server vs Client Components in the App Router.

## The mental models that answer most questions
- **UI = f(state).** A component is a function of props and state; React re-runs it when they change and commits the minimal DOM changes.
- **Render is pure, effects synchronise.** Rendering only computes; side effects go in event handlers or effects with cleanup.
- **Identity matters.** Same element type + same key = same component instance (state kept). Object/function identity (`Object.is`) decides whether memo and effect dependencies see a change.
- **Server first in Next.js.** Fetch data in Server Components, push `'use client'` down to the interactive leaves.

## How to study this topic
- Build a tiny app: a todo list with keyed rows, a fetch hook with cleanup, a memoised list, then port it to the Next.js App Router.
- Open React DevTools → Profiler and watch which components re-render after each change.
- Practise saying the 30-second answer for each question, then the deeper explanation.

cheatsheet.title: Rendering
points: Trigger (batched) → render (pure) → reconcile → commit → paint; useEffect runs after commit (usually after paint)
Same type: keep node + state; different type: remount subtree
Keys identify list items; never index for reorderable lists, never Math.random()
A parent re-render re-renders its children by default

cheatsheet.title: State and props
points: Props are read-only inputs; state is owned memory changed via its setter
Data down, events up (callback props)
Updater form for derived updates: setCount(c => c + 1)
Compute derived values during render — do not store them

cheatsheet.title: Effects
points: No array: every commit; []: first commit; [a, b]: when a or b changes (Object.is)
Cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount
Strict Mode (dev): setup → cleanup → setup on mount
Abort/ignore stale fetches in cleanup

cheatsheet.title: Performance
points: memo skips a child when all props are Object.is-equal
useMemo caches a value; useCallback caches a function identity
Inline objects/functions defeat memo
Profile first; the React Compiler can auto-memoise

cheatsheet.title: State management
points: Local → lift up → Context (rarely changing) → Zustand/Redux Toolkit
Server state → TanStack Query / Server Components
Shareable UI state → URL search params

cheatsheet.title: Next.js App Router
points: Server Components by default: async, DB access, zero client JS
'use client' marks a module boundary; still pre-rendered on the server
Static by default; cookies()/headers()/no-store → dynamic
ISR: export const revalidate = 60; revalidatePath / revalidateTag
params and searchParams are Promises (await them)

questions.title: What is the Virtual DOM and how does reconciliation work?
questions.prompt: Explain what React's **Virtual DOM** is and what happens between `setState` and the screen updating. How does **reconciliation** (diffing) decide which real DOM nodes to keep, update, remove or create? What are the **render** and **commit** phases?
hints: A component returns a description of the UI (plain objects), not real DOM nodes.
On an update React gets a new description and compares it with the previous one. Comparing two arbitrary trees perfectly is very expensive — what shortcuts does React take?
Two heuristics: a different element type means "replace the subtree"; keys identify children in a list.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "The Virtual DOM is a copy of the DOM that makes React faster." Vague, and the "faster than the DOM" claim is misleading.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Describe elements as JS objects, the render → reconcile → commit pipeline, the two diffing heuristics (type and key) that make it O(n), batching, and that only the minimal set of DOM operations is applied in the commit phase.

solution.summary: The Virtual DOM is the tree of plain JavaScript objects (React elements) that your components return. When state changes, React re-renders to get a new tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation) using two heuristics — different element type means replace, and keys match list children — and then commits only the necessary DOM changes in one batch.
solution.explanation:
**Elements, not DOM nodes.** JSX like `

Count: {count}

` compiles to a call that returns an object: `{ type: 'h1', props: { children: ['Count: ', 2] } }`. A whole screen is a tree of such objects — cheap to create and compare. React keeps the current tree internally as **fiber** nodes (one unit of work per component/element). **What happens after `setState`** 1. **Trigger** — state updates are queued and **batched** (React 18+ batches automatically, even in timeouts and promises), so the two updates in `handleClick` cause one re-render. 2. **Render phase** — React calls the affected components again to get a new element tree. This must be **pure** (no DOM changes, no side effects); in concurrent rendering it can be paused or thrown away. 3. **Reconciliation** — the new tree is compared with the previous one, top-down: - **Same type** (`
` vs `
`) → keep the DOM node (and component state), update only changed props, recurse into children. - **Different type** (`

` vs ``, or `` vs ``) → destroy the old subtree, including its state, and build a new one. - **Lists** → children are matched by **key**, so inserting at the top moves nothing and creates one node. 4. **Commit phase** — React applies the collected DOM operations synchronously, attaches refs and runs `useLayoutEffect`; then the browser paints. `useEffect` callbacks run after the commit — usually after the paint, although for updates caused by a discrete input such as a click React 18+ runs them before the paint. **Why heuristics?** An exact minimal diff of two trees is roughly O(n³). With the type and key rules React's diff is **O(n)**, and in practice these rules match how UIs change. **Is the Virtual DOM "faster than the DOM"?** Not inherently — a perfectly hand-written DOM update is always at least as fast. Its value is the programming model: you describe the UI for the current state, and React computes and batches a small set of updates for you. Tools like the **React Compiler** (automatic memoisation) reduce the render work further.
keyPoints: Virtual DOM = lightweight tree of React elements (plain objects) returned by components
Pipeline: trigger (batched) → render (pure, may be interrupted) → reconcile → commit (DOM changes) → paint; useEffect runs after the commit (usually after the paint)
Same type: keep node and state, patch props; different type: unmount and rebuild the subtree
Keys let React match list children across renders
Heuristics make diffing O(n) instead of O(n³)

pitfalls: Claiming the Virtual DOM is always faster than direct DOM manipulation
Defining a component inside another component — its type changes every render, so its subtree and state are destroyed each time
Doing side effects (fetching, subscriptions, DOM writes) during render instead of in effects or event handlers
Using unstable keys (index for reorderable lists, Math.random()) that defeat the list diff

followUps.question: What is React Fiber?
followUps.answer: The reconciler rewrite (React 16+) that represents the tree as linked fiber nodes, so rendering work can be split into units, paused, prioritised (e.g. useTransition) and resumed. The commit phase is still synchronous.

followUps.question: How do you reset a component's state on purpose?
followUps.answer: Give it a different key (<Profile key={userId} />): a new key means a new identity, so React unmounts the old instance and mounts a fresh one.

questions.title: useEffect: the dependency array and the cleanup function
questions.prompt: Explain how `useEffect` works. When does the effect run with **no** dependency array, with `[]`, and with `[a, b]`? What is the **cleanup function**, and exactly when does React call it? Use a chat room that connects to `roomId` as the example, and mention common bugs (missing dependencies, stale closures, fetch race conditions).
hints: Effects run after React has committed the render to the screen, never during rendering.
React compares each dependency with its previous value using Object.is. What if nothing changed?
Before running an effect again — and when the component unmounts — React first runs the previous cleanup.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "[] means componentDidMount and the return is componentWillUnmount." Lifecycle thinking that breaks as soon as a dependency changes.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Think in synchronisation: the effect keeps an external system in sync with props/state. Explain when it runs for each deps form, that cleanup runs before every re-run and on unmount with the old values, Object.is comparison, and how to fix stale closures and fetch races.

solution.summary: useEffect runs a side effect after React commits a render. With no array it runs after every commit, with [] only after the first, and with [a, b] after commits where any dependency changed (compared with Object.is). If the effect returns a function, React calls that cleanup before running the effect again and when the component unmounts, so each effect can undo its own work (disconnect, unsubscribe, abort).
solution.explanation:
**Mental model: synchronisation, not lifecycle.** An effect says "keep this external system (socket, subscription, timer, document title) in sync with these values". React handles *when*.

**When does it run?**
| Dependency array | Effect runs | Cleanup runs |
|---|---|---|
| none | after **every** commit | before every re-run + on unmount |
| `[]` | after the **first** commit only | on unmount |
| `[roomId]` | after commits where `roomId` changed | before each re-run (with the **old** `roomId`) + on unmount |

Dependencies are compared with `Object.is`. Objects and functions created during render are **new every render**, so `[options]` re-runs every time — move them inside the effect, memoise them, or depend on primitive fields.

**Order on a change** (`roomId: 'general' → 'jobs'`): render → commit DOM → **cleanup of the old effect** (disconnect from general — the cleanup closed over the old `roomId`) → **new effect** (connect to jobs).

**Common bugs**
1. **Missing dependency** — using `roomId` inside but listing `[]`: the effect never re-syncs, you stay connected to the old room. Let the `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule guide you.
2. **Stale closure** — a `setInterval` callback reading `count` from the first render. Use the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` or include the dependency.
3. **Fetch race condition** — the response for an old id arrives after the new one. In cleanup, set an `ignore` flag or call `controller.abort()`.
4. **Infinite loop** — an effect that sets state it also depends on, without a condition.
5. **Effect not needed at all** — values computable from props/state should be computed during render; user-triggered work belongs in event handlers.

**Related:** `useLayoutEffect` runs before the browser paints (for measuring layout); in development Strict Mode, React deliberately runs effect → cleanup → effect once on mount to check your cleanup.
keyPoints: Effects run after commit; no array = every commit, [] = first commit, [deps] = when a dep changes
Dependencies are compared with Object.is — new objects/functions each render cause re-runs
Cleanup runs before the next run (with the old values) and on unmount
Every value from the component used inside the effect belongs in the deps (exhaustive-deps)
Use cleanup to avoid leaks and races: disconnect, unsubscribe, clearInterval, abort

followUps.question: How do you avoid a race condition when fetching in an effect?
followUps.answer: Create an AbortController (or an ignore flag) inside the effect and abort / set ignore = true in the cleanup, so a slow response for an old id is never applied.

followUps.question: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect?
followUps.answer: useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before paint, so it can measure layout and update without flicker; it blocks painting, so use useEffect by default.

questions.title: Why do lists need keys, and why is the index a bad key?
questions.prompt: React warns "Each child in a list should have a unique key prop". What does the key do during reconciliation? Show what goes wrong with `key={index}` when an item is inserted at the top of a list whose rows have their own state (for example a text input), and what makes a good key.
hints: After a re-render React must decide which old row corresponds to which new row.
With index keys, "row 0" is always the first position — whatever data is now there.
Component state belongs to the instance React matched, not to the data you think it belongs to.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Keys make lists faster / remove the warning." Does not explain identity or the state bug.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explain that keys give list children a stable identity across renders, show the insert-at-top bug with index keys (state sticks to the wrong row, extra DOM work), and give the rules: stable, unique among siblings, from the data — plus the key-to-reset-state trick.

solution.summary: A key is a list child's identity across renders: React matches old and new children by key, then keeps, moves, creates or removes them. With key={index}, identity follows the position, so inserting at the top makes every row "become" a different item — their state (typed input, focus, animations) stays at the old position. Use a stable unique id from the data.
solution.explanation:
**What the key is for.** When a list re-renders, React compares the new children with the old ones. Without keys it can only match by position. With keys it matches **by identity**: "the child with key `m` is the same component as before", even if it moved.

**The index-key bug** (see the visual)
1. Rows are `Milk` (key 0) and `Eggs` (key 1). The user types "2 litres" into Milk's input — that text lives in the **row instance's state**.
2. Bread is inserted at the top. New keys are 0, 1, 2 for Bread, Milk, Eggs.
3. React sees key 0 still exists → **reuses** the instance that held "2 litres" and just gives it `text="Bread"`. Now Bread shows Milk's note. Key 1 (old Eggs row) receives "Milk", key 2 is new.
4. Result: wrong state, plus extra DOM text updates for every row.

With `key={todo.id}`, React matches `m → m` and `e → e`, inserts one new row for `b`, and the note stays with Milk.

**Rules for keys**
- **Stable** — the same item always gets the same key (a database id, a slug, a UUID created when the item is created).
- **Unique among siblings** (not globally).
- **Not `Math.random()` or `crypto.randomUUID()` during render** — every render creates new keys, so every row is unmounted and remounted (lost state, lost focus, slow).
- The index is acceptable only if the list is static: never reordered, filtered or inserted into, and rows have no state.

**Keys outside lists.** Changing a component's key forces React to treat it as a new component: `<ProfileForm key={userId} />` resets the whole form when the user changes — a clean way to reset state without effects.
keyPoints: Keys give list children an identity so React can match old and new children
State belongs to the matched instance — wrong keys move state to the wrong item
Index keys break on insert/reorder/filter; random keys remount everything
Use a stable id from the data, unique among siblings
Changing a key on purpose resets a component's state

visuals.title: Insert "Bread" at the top: index keys vs id keys
visuals.caption: Each column is one rendered row. The third row is the state that lives inside that row's component instance.

steps.note: Using `key={index}`. Two rows; the user typed "2 litres" into **Milk**'s input. That text is stored in the state of the instance with key `0`.
Bread is added at the top. The new keys by position are `0, 1, 2`. React sees key `0` again and **reuses** that instance — with its state — for Bread.
Result: **Bread shows Milk's note**, and Milk's row lost it. React also had to change the text of rows 0 and 1 and create row 2 — more DOM work than needed.
Same scenario with `key={todo.id}`: Milk's instance has key `m` and holds "2 litres".
After inserting Bread the keys are `b, m, e`. React matches `m → m` and `e → e` (same instances and DOM nodes, untouched) and creates **one** new row for `b`.
The note stays with **Milk** where it belongs. Stable keys keep state attached to the data, not to the position.

pitfalls: Using the index as key for lists that can be sorted, filtered or prepended to
Generating keys during render with Math.random() or randomUUID()
Putting the key on the wrong element (it belongs on the outermost element returned by map, e.g. the component or Fragment)
Thinking keys must be globally unique — they only need to be unique among siblings

followUps.question: Can you read props.key inside the child?
followUps.answer: No. key (like ref in older React) is consumed by React and not passed as a prop; pass the id separately if the child needs it.

followUps.question: How do you add a key to a Fragment in a list?
followUps.answer: Use the long form <Fragment key={item.id}>...</Fragment>; the short <>...</> syntax cannot take a key.

questions.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled components
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a **controlled** and an **uncontrolled** input in React? How do you read the value in each case, what are the trade-offs, and which would you choose for a login form, a live-search box and a file upload?
hints: Ask: who owns the current value — React state or the DOM element?
Controlled inputs use value + onChange; uncontrolled ones use defaultValue and a ref or FormData.
A file input's value can only be set by the user, never by your code.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Controlled uses state, uncontrolled uses refs." Correct but no reasoning about data flow, re-renders or when to use which.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explain the source of truth, the data flow on each keystroke, what each enables (instant validation/formatting vs fewer re-renders and simpler code), React 19 form actions with FormData, file inputs, and the controlled/uncontrolled switching warning.

solution.summary: In a controlled component React state is the source of truth: the input shows value={state} and every keystroke goes through onChange → setState → re-render. In an uncontrolled component the DOM keeps the value and you read it when needed with a ref or FormData (often on submit). Controlled gives instant validation and formatting; uncontrolled is simpler and re-renders less.
solution.explanation:
**Controlled**
- `<input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />`
- Data flow per keystroke: DOM event → `onChange` → `setEmail` → re-render → React writes the value back to the input.
- Because every change passes through your code, you can **validate as the user types**, transform input (trim, uppercase, mask a phone number), disable the submit button, or keep several fields in sync.
- Cost: a re-render on every keystroke (fine for most forms; matters for very large forms).
- `value` without `onChange` (and without `readOnly`) creates a field the user cannot edit, and React warns.

**Uncontrolled**
- `<input defaultValue="" ref={inputRef} />` or just `name="email"` inside a `<form>`.
- The DOM stores the value; React does not re-render while typing. Read it on demand: `inputRef.current.value` or `new FormData(form)`.
- **React 19 form actions** make this the natural choice for simple forms: `<form action={signup}>` receives a `FormData` object, works with `useActionState`/`useFormStatus`, and React resets uncontrolled fields after a successful action.
- **File inputs are always uncontrolled** — for security, only the user can choose a file.
- Form libraries like React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs + refs for performance.

**Choosing**
- Login form → uncontrolled + form action / FormData is enough (validate on submit, use `required`/`type="email"`).
- Live search, character counter, formatted inputs → controlled.
- File upload → uncontrolled (ref or FormData).

**Pitfall:** switching from uncontrolled to controlled (`value={user.name}` where `user.name` starts `undefined`) triggers a warning — initialise state with `''`.
keyPoints: Controlled = value from React state + onChange; uncontrolled = DOM owns the value (defaultValue)
Controlled enables instant validation/formatting at the cost of a re-render per keystroke
Read uncontrolled values with a ref or FormData; React 19 form actions receive FormData
File inputs are always uncontrolled
Never switch an input between controlled and uncontrolled (initialise state to "")

questions.title: Props vs state
questions.prompt: What is the difference between **props** and **state** in React? Who owns each, who can change them, and what triggers a re-render? Explain one-way data flow and how a child can change data that lives in its parent ("lifting state up").
hints: Think of a component as a function: what are its parameters, and what is its private memory?
Can a child modify the props it receives?
If two components need the same data, move it to their closest common parent and pass a callback down.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Props are passed in, state is internal." True but no data flow, no re-render rules, no example of a child updating a parent.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Define both, stress that props are read-only and state changes only through its setter, show data down / events up with a callback prop, explain lifting state up and that a parent re-render re-renders its children with new props.

solution.summary: Props are the inputs a parent passes to a component — read-only from the child's point of view. State is data a component owns and changes over time with its setter; changing state re-renders that component and its children. Data flows down as props and changes flow up through callback props, so the owner of the state is the only one who changes it.
solution.explanation:
**Props** — like function parameters.
- Passed by the parent: `<Display count={count} />`.
- **Read-only**: a component must never modify its props (`props.count++` is a bug — React components must be pure with respect to their props).
- Can be any value: strings, objects, JSX (`children`), and **functions** (callbacks).

**State** — the component's memory between renders.
- Created with `useState` / `useReducer` and owned by one component.
- Changed **only** through the setter (`setCount`), never by assignment. Calling the setter schedules a re-render of the owner.
- Updates are applied on the next render (the variable does not change immediately); use the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` when the new value depends on the old one.

**One-way data flow**
1. `Parent` owns `count` and passes it down as a prop.
2. `IncrementButton` cannot change `count`, so the parent passes a **callback** (`onIncrement`).
3. The click calls the callback → `setCount` in the parent → the parent re-renders → `Display` receives the new prop.

**Lifting state up.** When two siblings need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent and pass it (and the updater) down. If many distant components need it, consider composition, Context or a store.

**Don't store derived data in state.** If a value can be computed from props or other state (a filtered list, a full name, a total), compute it during render — duplicated state gets out of sync.

questions.title: What is prop drilling, and when should you use Context?
questions.prompt: What is **prop drilling**, and why is it a problem? Show how **Context** (`createContext`, a provider, `useContext`) solves it, what it costs in terms of re-renders, and what other options exist (component composition, a state library).
hints: Picture a value that is needed four levels down, but the components in between do not use it.
Context lets a deep component read a value from the nearest provider above it.
Every consumer re-renders when the provider value changes — and a new object literal is a new value every render.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Use Context or Redux to avoid passing props." Treats Context as a state manager and ignores composition and re-render costs.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Define prop drilling and when it is fine, show composition (children/slots) as the first fix, Context for widely needed, rarely changing data (theme, user, locale), its re-render behaviour and how to limit it (memoised value, split contexts), and when a store fits better.

solution.summary: Prop drilling is passing a prop through intermediate components that do not use it, just to reach a deep child. It couples those components to data they do not care about. Context lets any component read a value from the nearest provider above it without passing props; it fits app-wide, rarely changing data (current user, theme, locale). Every consumer re-renders when the value changes, so keep the value stable and consider composition or a store for frequently changing state.
solution.explanation:
**Prop drilling.** `App → Layout → Sidebar → UserBadge`: only `UserBadge` uses `user`, but `Layout` and `Sidebar` must accept and forward it. Two or three levels is fine and explicit. It becomes a problem when many layers forward many props, refactors touch every layer, and components become hard to reuse.

**Fix 1 — composition (try this first).** Let the parent build the deep element and pass it as `children` or a "slot" prop: `<Layout sidebar={<UserBadge user={user} />} />`. The intermediate components render whatever they get and never see `user`.

**Fix 2 — Context.**
1. `const UserContext = createContext(defaultValue)`.
2. Provide: `<UserContext value={user}>...</UserContext>` (React 19; earlier versions use `<UserContext.Provider value={user}>`).
3. Consume anywhere below: `useContext(UserContext)` (or `use(UserContext)` in React 19, which can also be called conditionally).
A component reads the value from the **nearest** provider above it; without one, it gets the default.

**Re-render cost.** When the provider's `value` changes (by `Object.is`), **every component that reads that context re-renders**, even if a memoised parent in between skipped rendering. Two common mistakes:
- `value={{ user, setUser }}` creates a new object every render → all consumers re-render every time. Wrap it in `useMemo`.
- One giant context for everything → a change to any field re-renders all consumers. **Split** contexts (e.g. `UserContext` and `ThemeContext`, or state vs dispatch).

**When to use something else.** Context is a *transport* mechanism, not a state manager. For frequently updated, widely shared client state (cart, filters, editor state) a store such as **Zustand** or **Redux Toolkit** lets components subscribe to just the slice they need. For data from the server use **TanStack Query** or Server Components.

Composition (children/slots) often removes drilling without any new API
Context: createContext → provider with value → useContext/use in any descendant
All consumers re-render when the value changes; memoise the value and split contexts
Context suits rarely changing global data; use a store or a server-state library for the rest

questions.title: useMemo vs useCallback vs React.memo
questions.prompt: What do `React.memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` each do? Why does a `memo` child still re-render when the parent passes an inline function, and how does `useCallback` fix it? When is memoisation a waste?
hints: One of them wraps a component, the other two are hooks that cache something between renders.
memo compares old and new props one by one with Object.is. Is () => {} === () => {}?
useCallback(fn, deps) is the same as useMemo(() => fn, deps).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "They make React faster, so use them everywhere." No understanding of reference equality, and over-memoising adds cost and complexity.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explain that a parent render re-renders children by default, that memo skips a child when all props are Object.is-equal, that useMemo caches a computed value and useCallback caches a function identity so memo can work, and when to measure instead of memoising (React DevTools Profiler, React Compiler).

solution.summary: React.memo wraps a component and skips re-rendering it when every prop is Object.is-equal to last time. useMemo caches the result of a calculation between renders until its dependencies change; useCallback caches a function so its identity stays the same. They work together: inline objects and functions are new on every render, which defeats memo, so you stabilise them with useMemo/useCallback.
solution.explanation:
**Default behaviour.** When a component re-renders, React re-renders **all of its children**, whether their props changed or not. That is usually fast enough.

**`React.memo(Component)`** — before re-rendering, React compares each new prop with the old one using `Object.is`. If all are equal, it reuses the last result and skips the child (and its subtree). Its own state or context changes still re-render it.

**`useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b])`** — runs `compute` on the first render and again only when `a` or `b` changes; otherwise returns the cached value. Two uses:
1. Skip an **expensive calculation** (filtering/sorting thousands of rows).
2. Keep a **stable reference** for an object/array passed to a memoised child or used as an effect dependency.

**`useCallback(fn, deps)`** — returns the **same function object** until a dependency changes. It does not make the function faster; it keeps its identity stable so `memo` children and effect dependencies do not see "a new function" every render. Equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

**Why the inline function breaks memo** (see the visual): `() => {}` creates a new function every render and `Object.is(newFn, oldFn)` is `false`, so `ProductList` re-renders even though nothing meaningful changed. The same happens with `style={{...}}` or `options={[...]}` literals.

**When it is a waste**
- The child is cheap to render, or its props change on almost every render anyway.
- Memoising primitives (strings, numbers already compare by value).
- Dependencies that change every render (the cache never hits, but you still pay for the comparison).
Measure with the React DevTools **Profiler** first. The **React Compiler** can add this memoisation automatically at build time, which removes most hand-written `useMemo`/`useCallback`.

useMemo caches a computed value; useCallback caches a function identity

`memo` compares the props: `Object.is` is true for both, so React **skips** `ProductList` and its whole subtree.
**What if** `onSelect={(id) => console.log(id)}` were written inline? Every render creates function #2, #3… → `Object.is` fails → `ProductList` re-renders anyway and `memo` is useless.
Typing "p" changes `query` → `useMemo` recomputes a **new** array, so `products` changed and `ProductList` correctly re-renders with the filtered items.

followUps.question: Does memo prevent re-renders caused by context or the component's own state?
followUps.answer: No. memo only short-circuits re-renders that come from the parent with equal props; state and context changes inside the child still re-render it.

followUps.question: Can you customise memo's comparison?
followUps.answer: Yes, memo(Component, arePropsEqual) takes a custom comparator, but deep comparisons can cost more than the render they save.

questions.title: What are custom hooks? Write useFetch
questions.prompt: What is a **custom hook**, and what problem does it solve? Write a `useFetch(url)` hook that returns `{ data, error, loading }`, cancels stale requests when the URL changes, and explain whether two components that call it share state. Mention the **rules of hooks**.
hints: A custom hook is just a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks.
Each call to a hook gets its own state slot — hooks share logic, not data.
For useFetch: useState for the result, useEffect keyed on url, and an AbortController in the cleanup.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "A custom hook is a shared state between components." Wrong: every call has its own state.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Define it (use-prefixed function calling hooks), explain reuse of stateful logic with independent state per call, implement useFetch with an effect, cleanup via AbortController and derived loading, and mention rules of hooks and when to use TanStack Query instead.

solution.summary: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and which calls other hooks, so stateful logic (fetching, subscriptions, form handling, debouncing) can be reused across components. It shares the logic, not the state: every component that calls useFetch gets its own independent state and effect.
solution.explanation:
**Why custom hooks?** Before hooks, logic reuse needed higher-order components or render props, which nested wrappers ("wrapper hell"). A custom hook is plain function composition: `useFetch` uses `useState` and `useEffect`, and components call `useFetch`.

**How `useFetch` works**
1. `useState` stores the last finished result **together with the URL it belongs to**.
2. `useEffect(..., [url])` starts a request after each commit where `url` changed, with an `AbortController`.
3. The cleanup calls `controller.abort()` when `url` changes or the component unmounts. A slow response for an old URL can never overwrite the new one (no race condition) and no state is set after unmount.
4. `loading` is **derived** during render (`result.url !== url`), so there is no extra state to keep in sync and no synchronous `setState` inside the effect.
5. `AbortError` is ignored because it is expected; real errors (network, non-2xx) are stored.

**State is per call.** `UserCard` and `OrderCount` both call `useFetch`; React stores each call's state in that component's own hook slots, so they load, fail and update independently (see the visual). To *share* data, lift it up, use Context, or use a cache library.

**Rules of hooks** (custom hooks follow them too)
- Call hooks only at the **top level** of a component or another hook — not in loops, conditions or after an early return — because React identifies hooks by **call order**.
- Call hooks only from React function components or custom hooks.
- Name custom hooks `useSomething` so the linter can check these rules.

**Production note.** For real apps, a server-state library such as **TanStack Query** or SWR gives caching, de-duplication of identical requests, retries, background refetching and invalidation on top of exactly this pattern. In the Next.js App Router, prefer fetching in **Server Components** when the data is needed for the first render.
keyPoints: Custom hook = use-prefixed function that calls other hooks to reuse stateful logic
Each call has its own state — hooks share logic, not data
useFetch: state + effect on [url] + AbortController cleanup to prevent races and leaks
Derive values (loading) during render instead of syncing extra state
Follow the rules of hooks; prefer TanStack Query / Server Components for real data fetching

steps.note: `UserCard` and `OrderCount` mount with `id = 7`. Each `useFetch` call creates its **own** `result` state. `result.url` is `null`, so `loading` is derived as `true`.
After the commit, each component's effect runs and starts its own request with its own `AbortController`.
The user response arrives first. Only **UserCard's** `setResult` is called, so only `UserCard` re-renders; `OrderCount` is still loading.
The orders response arrives and updates **OrderCount's** state: 3 orders. Same hook, separate state.

The user selects `id = 9` (slow API). During render `url` no longer matches `result.url`, so `loading` is `true` **immediately** — no extra `setState` needed. Cleanups run (nothing pending), new requests start.
Before those answer, the user picks `id = 12`. The **cleanup aborts** both `/9` requests, so their late responses can never overwrite the screen (no race condition), and `/12` requests start.
The `/12` responses arrive and are applied. The aborted requests rejected with `AbortError`, which the hook deliberately ignores.

followUps.question: Why use TanStack Query instead of useFetch?
followUps.answer: It caches by key and shares the cache across components, de-duplicates identical requests, retries, refetches on focus/reconnect, and supports mutations with invalidation — all of which you would otherwise write yourself.

questions.title: CSR vs SSR vs SSG vs ISR (in Next.js)
questions.prompt: Compare **client-side rendering (CSR)**, **server-side rendering (SSR)**, **static site generation (SSG)** and **incremental static regeneration (ISR)**. When is the HTML produced in each, what does the user see first, how fresh is the data, and what does each cost? How do you choose each one in the **Next.js App Router**, and which would you use for a product page, a logged-in dashboard and a blog?
hints: Ask one question for each strategy: WHEN is the HTML generated — in the browser, per request, at build time, or at build time and then refreshed?
Think about what the first response contains: an empty shell, or real content?
ISR = static pages that are regenerated in the background after a time window (stale-while-revalidate).

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "SSR is better for SEO and CSR is a SPA." No timing, no freshness/cost trade-offs, no mapping to Next.js APIs.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Answer by when the HTML is generated, what the user sees first (FCP) vs when it becomes interactive (hydration), data freshness, server cost and SEO, map each to App Router features (static by default, dynamic APIs / no-store, revalidate, generateStaticParams, use client) and pick per page.

solution.summary: The difference is when the HTML is generated. CSR builds it in the browser after downloading JavaScript; SSR renders it on the server for every request; SSG renders it once at build time and serves it from a CDN; ISR is SSG whose pages are regenerated in the background after a revalidate window. In the Next.js App Router routes are static by default, become dynamic (SSR) when they use request data, use ISR with revalidate, and Client Components handle browser-only interactivity.
solution.explanation:
**CSR — client-side rendering.** The server sends an almost empty HTML shell plus a JS bundle; the browser runs React, fetches data, then renders. *Pros:* cheap static hosting, rich interactivity. *Cons:* blank/loading screen until JS + data arrive (slow first content on weak phones and networks), weaker SEO and link previews. Good for parts behind a login that change constantly (live stock, chat).

**SSR — server-side rendering.** For **every request** the server fetches data and renders HTML, so the first response already contains content; then the browser downloads JS and **hydrates** (attaches event handlers). *Pros:* always-fresh, personalised, SEO-friendly. *Cons:* server work and latency on every request (TTFB depends on your slowest query). Good for dashboards, search results, personalised pages.

**SSG — static site generation.** HTML is rendered **once at build time** and served from a CDN. *Pros:* fastest possible response, near-zero server cost, great SEO. *Cons:* data is as old as the last build; a rebuild is needed to change it. Good for docs, blogs, marketing pages.

**ISR — incremental static regeneration.** Static pages with an expiry: after the **revalidate window** (e.g. 60 s), the next request still gets the cached page **instantly**, while Next.js regenerates it in the background; later visitors get the fresh version (stale-while-revalidate). Pages that were not pre-built can be generated on first request and then cached. You can also revalidate **on demand** with `revalidatePath` / `revalidateTag` (e.g. after an admin edits a price). Good for e-commerce product pages, news.

**In the Next.js App Router** (Server Components by default)
- **Static (SSG)** is the default when a route uses no request-time data.
- **Dynamic (SSR)** when it uses request-time APIs such as `cookies()`, `headers()` or `searchParams`, or `fetch(url, { cache: 'no-store' })`.
- **ISR**: `export const revalidate = 60` in the route, or `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } })`; `generateStaticParams` pre-builds dynamic routes.
- **CSR**: a `'use client'` component that fetches in `useEffect` (or with TanStack Query/SWR) after hydration.
- With Next.js 16's opt-in **Cache Components**, the same ideas are expressed with the `'use cache'` directive and `cacheLife`.

**Mix per page:** a product page = ISR for name/price/description + a client component for the live "only 3 left" counter; the dashboard = SSR; the blog = SSG.

SSR/SSG/ISR send real content in the first response; hydration makes it interactive later
Trade-off triangle: freshness vs speed (TTFB) vs server cost

**SSG:** the HTML was rendered at build time, so a CDN returns it almost immediately. The trade-off is that the data is as old as the last build.
**ISR:** as fast as SSG for the visitor. If the `revalidate` window has passed, the cached page is still served instantly and the server regenerates a fresh copy in the background.

followUps.question: What is hydration?
followUps.answer: React running in the browser over server-rendered HTML, attaching event handlers and state so the page becomes interactive. The server HTML and the first client render must match, otherwise React reports a hydration mismatch.

followUps.question: What is streaming SSR?
followUps.answer: Sending the HTML in chunks: the shell is sent immediately and slow parts wrapped in <Suspense> (or loading.js) stream in when their data is ready, so one slow query does not block the whole page.

questions.title: Server Components vs Client Components (Next.js App Router)
questions.prompt: In the Next.js App Router, what is the difference between a **Server Component** and a **Client Component**? What does `'use client'` actually do, what can each kind of component do (and not do), what is sent to the browser, and how can a Server Component be rendered inside a Client Component?
hints: In the App Router, which kind is the default?
Server Components never run in the browser. What does that allow (DB, secrets) and forbid (state, effects, onClick)?
'use client' marks a boundary in the module graph, not a single component. Client Components are still pre-rendered to HTML on the server.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Server Components run on the server and Client Components run on the client." Misses that Client Components also render on the server for the first load, and cannot explain boundaries or serialisable props.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explain the default (server), capabilities of each, what ships to the browser (HTML + RSC payload + JS only for client modules), the use client boundary and its import graph, serialisable props, the children pattern, and server-only data access with Server Actions for mutations.

solution.summary: In the App Router every component is a Server Component unless its module (or a parent module) starts with 'use client'. Server Components run only on the server: they can be async, query the database and use secrets, and their code is never shipped to the browser, but they cannot use state, effects or event handlers. Client Components are pre-rendered to HTML on the server too, then hydrated in the browser, so they can use hooks and events.
solution.explanation:
**Server Components (default)**
- Run on the server, at build time or per request. They can be `async` and `await` data directly (database, file system, internal APIs, secrets).
- Their code and dependencies (ORM, markdown parser, date library) **stay on the server** — zero JS for them in the bundle.
- They cannot use `useState`, `useEffect`, event handlers like `onClick`, or browser APIs (`window`, `localStorage`).
- Their output is sent as the **RSC payload** (a serialised description of the rendered tree) plus HTML for the first load.

**Client Components (`'use client'`)**
- The directive at the top of a file marks a **boundary**: that module *and everything it imports* becomes part of the client bundle.
- They are still **rendered to HTML on the server** for the first page load, then **hydrated** in the browser, where they can use state, effects, refs, event handlers and browser APIs.
- Put the boundary as **low** in the tree as possible: make the "Add to cart" button a client component, not the whole page.

**Crossing the boundary**
- Props from a Server to a Client Component must be **serialisable** (strings, numbers, plain objects, arrays, Dates, Promises…). Functions cannot be passed — except **Server Actions** (`'use server'` functions) that the client can call to mutate data.
- A Client Component **cannot import** a Server Component (the import would turn it into client code), but it **can render one passed as `children`** or another prop. In `<Tabs><Reviews /></Tabs>`, `Reviews` is rendered by the server parent; `Tabs` only decides where to place it.
- Keep secrets safe with the `server-only` package: importing such a module from client code fails the build.

**Why it matters:** less JavaScript to download and hydrate (faster on mid-range phones), data fetching next to the data source without an extra API layer, and secrets that never reach the browser.
keyPoints: App Router components are Server Components by default
Server Components: async, direct DB/secret access, zero client JS; no state, effects or event handlers
'use client' marks a module boundary; Client Components are pre-rendered on the server and hydrated in the browser
Props across the boundary must be serialisable; Server Actions are the exception for functions
Server Components can be passed into Client Components as children; keep client boundaries small (leaves)

`'use client'` at the top of `SearchBox`, `AddToCartButton` and `Tabs` marks **boundaries**: those modules (and anything they import) become Client Components.
On the server, `ProductPage` **awaits the database directly**. The DB client and query code never leave the server.

The server renders **everything** — including the Client Components — to HTML, and serialises the Server Component output as the RSC payload. Only the client modules' JS (plus the React/Next.js runtime) is sent to the browser.
In the browser the HTML shows immediately; then the client JS loads and React **hydrates** only the three Client Components, attaching their state and `onClick` handlers.
`Reviews` sits **inside** the client `Tabs` but stays a Server Component: the server page rendered it and passed it as `children`. `Tabs` only decides where to place it.
Props that cross into a Client Component must be **serialisable**: `productId` (a string) is fine; a function like `onAdd={() => ...}` is not, unless it is a Server Action.

followUps.question: How do you mutate data from a Client Component without writing an API route?
followUps.answer: Use a Server Action: an async function marked 'use server' that the client can call (e.g. as a form action). It runs on the server, then you revalidate the affected paths/tags.

followUps.question: How do you make sure a module with secrets is never bundled for the client?
followUps.answer: Add import 'server-only' at the top. If any Client Component imports it (directly or indirectly), the build fails.

questions.title: How do you choose a state management approach in React?
questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: "How do you manage state in a React app — would you use Redux?" Explain the **different kinds of state** (local UI state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state) and when you would use `useState`/`useReducer`, lifting state up, Context, a store such as **Zustand** or **Redux Toolkit**, and **TanStack Query**.
hints: Not all state is the same: is it owned by the browser, or is it a cached copy of data that lives on a server?
Start with the smallest scope that works, and move up only when you need to share.
Server data needs caching, refetching and invalidation — a different problem from UI state.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "I put everything in Redux" or "Context replaces Redux." One tool for every problem, often copying server data into a global store by hand.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Classify state first, then pick the smallest tool: local state → lift up → Context for rarely changing globals → a store for frequently changing shared client state → TanStack Query (or Server Components) for server data → URL for shareable UI state. Explain re-render behaviour and trade-offs.

solution.summary: First classify the state, then use the smallest tool that fits. Local UI state lives in useState or useReducer; state shared by a few components is lifted to their common parent; rarely changing app-wide values (theme, current user) go in Context; frequently changing shared client state goes in a store like Zustand or Redux Toolkit; and data from the server is server state, best handled by TanStack Query (or fetched in Server Components), not copied into a global store.
solution.explanation:
**1. Classify the state**
| Kind | Example | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI state | modal open, input text, selected tab | `useState`, `useReducer` |
| Shared by nearby components | filters + list in the same page | lift state up |
| Global, rarely changing | theme, logged-in user, locale | Context |
| Global, frequently changing client state | cart, multi-step editor, notifications | Zustand, Redux Toolkit |
| Server state (a cache of remote data) | products, orders, profile | TanStack Query / SWR, Server Components |
| URL state | search query, page number, sort | `searchParams` / router |
| Form state | big validated forms | React Hook Form, React 19 form actions |

**2. Local first.** `useState` for independent values; `useReducer` when several values change together or the next state depends on an action type (cart add/remove/clear) — the reducer is a pure function that is easy to test.

**3. Context** removes prop drilling, but every consumer re-renders when the value changes, so it suits values that change rarely. It is a transport, not a state manager.

**4. Stores.** **Zustand** is a small hook-based store with no provider; components subscribe with a **selector** and re-render only when that slice changes. **Redux Toolkit** adds a predictable action/reducer model, excellent DevTools (time-travel), middleware and RTK Query — good for large teams and complex flows, at the cost of more structure.

**5. Server state is different.** It is owned by the server, can be stale, shared by many components, and needs loading/error states, caching, de-duplication, retries, background refetching and invalidation after mutations. **TanStack Query** gives all of that keyed by `queryKey`. Copying fetched data into Redux by hand re-implements this badly. In the Next.js App Router, data needed for the first render is often best fetched in **Server Components**.

**6. URL state** survives refresh and can be shared as a link — keep filters, pagination and tabs there.

**A good interview answer:** "I start with local state and lift it when needed, use Context for theme/auth, TanStack Query for anything from the API, and add Zustand or Redux Toolkit only when there is genuinely shared, frequently changing client state."
keyPoints: Classify first: local UI, shared client, server, URL, form state
Smallest scope that works: useState/useReducer → lift up → Context → store
Context for rarely changing globals; consumers re-render on every value change
Zustand/Redux Toolkit for frequently changing shared client state (selectors limit re-renders)
Server state belongs in TanStack Query/SWR or Server Components, not hand-copied into a store

followUps.question: When would you still choose Redux Toolkit over Zustand?
followUps.answer: Large teams that benefit from strict conventions (actions, reducers, slices), heavy use of middleware, time-travel debugging, or an existing Redux codebase. RTK Query also covers server state if you are already on Redux.

followUps.question: How do you update the UI after a mutation with TanStack Query?
followUps.answer: Use useMutation and, in onSuccess, call queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["orders", userId] }) (or update the cache with setQueryData for an optimistic update).

questions.title: Why does my useEffect run twice in development?
questions.prompt: A junior developer notices that `console.log` inside `useEffect(..., [])` prints **twice** and their API is called twice — but only in development. Why does React do this, does it happen in production, and what is the correct fix (and the wrong fixes)?
hints: Look for <StrictMode> in your entry file (Next.js App Router enables it by default).
React deliberately mounts, unmounts and mounts the component again in development.
If setup → cleanup → setup behaves differently from a single setup, your cleanup is missing or incomplete.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "It is a React bug; I add a useRef flag so the effect only runs once." Hides the missing cleanup the check was designed to reveal.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explain that Strict Mode in development runs an extra setup → cleanup → setup cycle on mount (and double-invokes render functions) to surface missing cleanup and impure renders, that production runs once, and that the fix is a correct cleanup (disconnect, unsubscribe, abort/ignore for fetches) or moving the logic out of an effect.

solution.summary: In development, <StrictMode> makes React mount every component, simulate an unmount (running effect cleanups) and mount it again, so each effect runs setup → cleanup → setup once on mount. It is a deliberate stress test for missing cleanup; production runs the effect once. The fix is a proper cleanup function, not a flag that skips the second run.
solution.explanation:
**What Strict Mode does (development only)**
- **Double-invokes rendering:** component bodies, `useState`/`useMemo`/`useReducer` initialisers and updater functions run twice, to catch impure rendering (mutating props, global variables).
- **Re-runs effects once on mount:** setup → **cleanup** → setup, as if the user left the screen and came back immediately.
- React 19 also double-invokes **ref callbacks** on mount in Strict Mode.
- None of this happens in **production builds**.

**Why?** Real apps mount and unmount components all the time: navigating away and back, tab switches, list filtering, Fast Refresh, and future features that preserve state while hiding UI. An effect without correct cleanup leaks — duplicate subscriptions, two sockets, intervals that tick twice as fast. Strict Mode makes that bug visible **immediately** instead of weeks later.

**Correct fixes**
1. **Write the cleanup** so setup → cleanup → setup ends in the same state as one setup: `disconnect()`, `unsubscribe()`, `clearInterval(id)`, `removeEventListener`.
2. **Fetching:** abort or ignore the first request in cleanup (`AbortController` or an `ignore` flag) so only the last response is used. The duplicate request in dev is harmless; better still, use TanStack Query (which de-duplicates) or fetch in a Server Component.
3. **Not an effect at all?** Work caused by a user action (e.g. "buy" → POST) belongs in the **event handler**, not in an effect — then it never runs twice. One-time app initialisation can live outside components (module level).

**Wrong fixes:** removing `<StrictMode>`, or a `useRef(false)` flag that skips the second run — both hide the real bug.

**Next.js:** Strict Mode is on by default in the App Router. `reactStrictMode` in `next.config.js` can switch it off (not recommended) and must be set to `true` to enable it for the Pages Router.
keyPoints: Development Strict Mode runs setup → cleanup → setup on mount; production runs once
It is a deliberate check for missing or wrong cleanup (and impure renders)
Fix with a correct cleanup: disconnect, unsubscribe, clear timers, abort/ignore fetches
User-triggered side effects belong in event handlers, not effects
Do not silence it with a ref flag or by removing StrictMode

visuals.caption: The open-connections panel should end with exactly one connection in every case.

steps.note: Development, inside `<StrictMode>`: React renders `ChatRoom` (calling the function body twice to check purity) and commits it. Effects have not run yet.
After the commit the effect runs for the first time: connect to 'general'.
Strict Mode now **simulates an unmount**: React calls the cleanup, which disconnects.
…and **mounts again**: the effect runs a second time. Net result: exactly **one** open connection — the same as production, so the component passes the check.

**Buggy version** (no cleanup returned): connect, nothing to undo, connect again → **two** sockets and every message arrives twice. Strict Mode exposed a leak that would also happen in production when the user leaves and returns.
**Production build:** no double render and no simulated unmount — the effect runs once. The cleanup still runs when the component really unmounts or `roomId` changes.

pitfalls: Adding a useRef "has run" flag to skip the second effect run
Removing <StrictMode> instead of fixing the cleanup
Sending POST requests (payments, orders) from an effect instead of the click handler
Assuming production behaves the same way and calls the API twice

followUps.question: Does Strict Mode slow down production?
followUps.answer: No. Its checks only run in development builds; <StrictMode> renders nothing extra in production.

followUps.question: My analytics "page view" effect fires twice in development. Is that a problem?
followUps.answer: Not in production, where it fires once. You can accept the dev duplicate, or send page views from the router/navigation event instead of a component effect.

quiz.question: What does the empty dependency array in useEffect(fn, []) mean?
options: Run the effect after every render
Run the effect after the first commit (mount) only; its cleanup runs on unmount
Never run the effect
Run the effect before the first render
quiz.explanation: With [] there are no dependencies that can change, so React runs the effect once after mounting and runs its cleanup when the component unmounts. (In development Strict Mode it also runs an extra setup → cleanup → setup cycle on mount.)

quiz.question: The button starts at 0. What does it show after ONE click?
quiz.explanation: All three calls read count from the same render, where it is 0, so each one sets 1. The updates are batched into one re-render showing 1. The updater form setCount(c => c + 1) would chain them and give 3.

quiz.question: Which change makes the counter above go up by 3 per click?
options: Use the updater form setCount((c) => c + 1) for each call
Wrap the three calls in a useEffect
Call forceUpdate() after each setCount
Add 'use client' to the file
quiz.explanation: An updater function receives the latest pending state, so the three updates are applied in sequence: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. Effects, forced updates or directives do not change how the stale count variable is read.

quiz.question: Why is key={index} a problem when items can be inserted at the top of a list?
options: React throws an error for numeric keys
Index keys disable re-rendering of the list
It makes every row render twice
Keys follow the position, so row state (like typed input) sticks to the wrong item
quiz.explanation: After an insert at the top, every item gets a different index. React matches by key, so the instance that used to be row 0 now renders the new first item but keeps its old state. A stable id from the data keeps state with the right item.

quiz.question: In development with <StrictMode>, an effect logs "connect" twice on mount. What is happening?
options: A bug in React 19 that is fixed in production patches
React mounts, simulates an unmount (running the cleanup) and mounts again to reveal missing cleanup; production runs it once
The dependency array is missing, so the effect runs on every render
The component is rendered once on the server and once in the browser
quiz.explanation: Strict Mode deliberately runs setup → cleanup → setup in development. If the cleanup undoes the setup, the end state is the same as running once. The fix for problems is a correct cleanup, not skipping the second run.

quiz.question: What does useCallback(fn, [a]) return?
options: The result of calling fn
A new function on every render
The same function reference between renders until a changes
A memoised component
quiz.explanation: useCallback caches the function object itself, so its identity is stable until a dependency changes. That is useful when the function is passed to a memo child or used as an effect dependency. It is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, [a]).

quiz.question: A child wrapped in React.memo still re-renders every time its parent renders. What is the most likely cause?
options: The parent passes a new object or inline function as a prop on each render
memo only works with class components
The child uses useState internally
memo is disabled in production builds
quiz.explanation: memo compares props with Object.is. An inline arrow function or object literal is a new reference on every parent render, so the comparison fails. Stabilise it with useCallback/useMemo (or let the React Compiler do it).

quiz.question: Which of these can a Next.js App Router Server Component do?
options: Use useState to track a counter
Attach an onClick handler to a button
Read window.localStorage
await a database query directly inside the component
quiz.explanation: Server Components run only on the server, can be async and can access databases and secrets directly. State, event handlers and browser APIs require a Client Component.

quiz.question: What does 'use client' at the top of a file do in the Next.js App Router?
options: Makes the component render only in the browser, with no server HTML
Marks a boundary: this module and the modules it imports become Client Components that are sent to the browser and hydrated
Disables server-side data fetching for the whole route
Turns the file into an API route handler
quiz.explanation: Client Components are still pre-rendered to HTML on the server for the first load; 'use client' means their code is also bundled for the browser and hydrated there so they can use state and events. The tempting first option is wrong because of that server pre-render.

quiz.question: A page exports `export const revalidate = 60`. A request arrives 2 minutes after the page was generated. What happens?
options: The request waits while the page is rebuilt
The page switches to rendering on every request
The cached (stale) page is served immediately and a fresh version is regenerated in the background
Next.js returns a 404 until the next deployment
quiz.explanation: That is ISR (stale-while-revalidate): the visitor gets the cached page instantly, regeneration happens in the background, and later visitors get the new page.

quiz.question: What happens with <input value={name} /> when there is no onChange and no readOnly?
options: Typing does not change the field, and React warns that value is set without onChange
It behaves like an uncontrolled input
React throws an error and stops rendering
The value is cleared after every keystroke
quiz.explanation: value makes the input controlled: React keeps forcing it to name. With no onChange, state never changes, so the field is effectively read-only and React logs a warning. Add onChange, use readOnly, or use defaultValue for an uncontrolled input.

quiz.question: A context provider's value changes. Which components re-render because of it?
options: Every component in the app
Only the provider component itself
Only components wrapped in React.memo
Every component below the provider that reads this context, even if a memoised parent skipped rendering
quiz.explanation: React finds all consumers of that context below the provider and re-renders them when the value is not Object.is-equal to the previous one. memo on an intermediate component does not block context updates. That is why the value should be memoised and large contexts split.
